concept.shortExplanation: Backpropagation answers one question for every weight in the network: if I nudge you, how much does the loss change? It gets those answers efficiently by applying the chain rule backwards from the output, reusing each layer's result for the layer beneath it. The gradients you will inspect here are the real ones, read straight out of the backward pass of the network you trained in the previous chapter — including the ones that vanish.
concept.ahaMoment: No weight is ever told what it should be. Each one only receives a signed number saying which way to move and how urgently, and the whole network coordinates through nothing more than that.

modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The in-browser network failed to initialise, so no gradients can be read. Reload the chapter to retry.

levels.title: Which Way Does It Move?
levels.instructions: For each highlighted edge, predict whether the gradient will push its weight up or down. Checked against the real signed gradient from the backward pass.
hints: The update rule is w ← w − lr·g. Only the *sign* of the gradient decides which way the weight moves — you never need its size for this question.

Subtracting a negative number pushes the weight up, so a negative gradient means the weight increases. Subtracting a positive number pushes it down, so a positive gradient means it decreases. That rule holds for every edge, regardless of layer.

Checked against this exact run (seed 13): the layer-2 edge from unit 3 to unit 1 carries a real gradient of −0.0274 — negative, so it increases. Apply the same sign check to whichever edge is highlighted.

levels.title: Rank the Gradients
levels.instructions: Order these edges by the magnitude of the gradient flowing through them, largest first. Scored by rank correlation against the real backward pass.
hints: Ignore the sign entirely — this is ranked by |gradient|, magnitude only. Compare how strongly the backward pass weighted each edge.

There's no shortcut like "later layers always carry the biggest gradient": the real magnitude is a product of downstream weights and activation derivatives multiplied together along the path back to that edge, and which edge wins can flip between rounds. Read the actual sizes rather than guessing from position in the network.

Checked against this exact run (seed 13), round 1's five edges ranked largest |gradient| first: layer 3 unit 1→1 (0.0433), layer 1 unit 2→2 (0.0086), layer 1 unit 2→4 (0.0038), layer 2 unit 1→4 (0.0033), layer 2 unit 2→2 (0.0003).

levels.title: The Vanishing Gradient
levels.instructions: A deep stack of sigmoids. Watch the gradient magnitude collapse as it travels backwards, then find the configuration change that keeps signal alive all the way to the first layer.
hints: This stack is five weight layers deep, and sigmoid's own derivative never exceeds 0.25 — every layer the backward pass crosses multiplies the signal by something smaller, so it shrinks fast on the way back. Try a different activation.

A rectifier's derivative is a flat 1 wherever the unit is active, so it doesn't shrink the signal layer over layer the way sigmoid does. Swapping the activation should let far more gradient survive the trip back to the first layer.

Measured directly on this exact net (seed 31): sigmoid gives a first-layer/last-layer ratio of about 0.001, well under the 0.05 floor. Switching to tanh reaches about 6.48, and relu or leakyRelu land around 0.34 — either clears even the 3-star band (0.3).
